summary: A country on the equator in East Africa, with the Great Rift Valley, the grasslands at the northern foot of Mount Kilimanjaro and abundant wildlife; it became independent from Britain in 1963 and is known for its long-distance runners.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: After British colonization in the late 19th century, Protestant groups such as the Church Missionary Society (Anglican), the Presbyterians and the Africa Inland Mission penetrated the Kenyan interior, using school-building as a means of evangelization, and those with a mission education became the elite of the colonial period and after independence. Many politicians, including Kenya's first president Kenyatta, attended mission schools, so Protestantism became widespread in the central and western regions.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: From the late 19th century, Catholic missions such as the Holy Ghost Fathers and the Consolata Missionaries set up mission stations, schools and hospitals in central and western Kenya, competing with Protestant influence. Catholicism has many followers among the Luhya, Luo and Kikuyu, and runs many secondary schools and medical institutions.

ranking.name: Evangelicals
ranking.description: Evangelical and Pentecostal churches expanded rapidly from the 1970s through missionaries from the United States and elsewhere, radio and large crusades, emphasizing experience of the Holy Spirit, divine healing and the "prosperity gospel", and especially attracting young people and the emerging middle class in cities such as Nairobi. Many new churches were founded by Kenyan pastors and can reach tens of thousands of members.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam came to the East African coast with Arab and Persian merchants from the 8th–9th centuries, and Swahili towns such as Mombasa and Lamu have been predominantly Muslim since the Middle Ages. Today Muslims are found mainly in the coastal region and the Somali areas of the northeast, and are a minority nationally.

ranking.name: African independent churches
ranking.description: From the early 20th century, some Kenyans, dissatisfied with missionaries' bans on traditional customs such as polygamy and circumcision, set up independent churches blending African culture, such as the Kikuyu independent schools and church movement of the 1920s and the African Israel Church Nineveh. These churches also played an important role in the anti-colonial movement.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Kenyan society is strongly religious, and those who explicitly call themselves non-religious are very few, appearing mainly among highly educated young people in big cities such as Nairobi.

religion.background: Kenya's indigenous peoples each have their own traditional beliefs; for example, the Kikuyu worship the deity Ngai, who dwells on Mount Kenya. Islam came to the East African coast with Arab and Persian merchants from the 8th–9th centuries, forming Swahili city-state culture. In 1844 the German missionary Krapf arrived in Mombasa, and after British colonial rule in the late 19th century, Protestant and Catholic missions set up schools and hospitals widely in the interior, and Christianity spread rapidly along with Western education. From the 20th century many indigenous churches combining Christianity and African culture appeared, and in recent decades Pentecostal and evangelical churches have grown rapidly.

language.official: The official languages are Swahili and English.

ranking.name: Kikuyu
ranking.description: The Kikuyu are Kenya's most numerous people, living mainly in the central highlands around Mount Kenya. In the colonial period the British set up the "White Highlands" on this fertile land, provoking the land question and the Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s; after independence Kikuyu politicians such as Kenyatta held power for a long time, and the Kikuyu language therefore has great influence in business and daily life in Nairobi.

ranking.name: Luhya
ranking.description: Luhya is the language of the Luhya people of western Kenya; it belongs to the Bantu family and in fact comprises more than ten closely related dialects. The Luhya are Kenya's second largest people, living mainly in agricultural regions of the west such as Kakamega and Bungoma.

ranking.name: Kalenjin
ranking.description: Kalenjin belongs to the Nilotic family and is a collective name for several closely related peoples of the Rift Valley region of western Kenya; the term "Kalenjin" was only used to unite these groups in the 1940s–50s. The Kalenjin are famous for producing world-class long-distance runners, and former president Moi and Ruto are both Kalenjin.

ranking.name: Luo
ranking.description: Luo belongs to the Nilotic family; the Luo migrated along the Nile from what is now South Sudan to the area around Lake Victoria around the 15th–16th centuries, living mainly in places such as Kisumu. The Luo have been very important in the independence movement and opposition politics, for example the Odinga family.

ranking.name: Swahili
ranking.description: Swahili originated on the East African coast, built on Bantu and absorbing many Arabic words; its native speakers are mainly the Swahili people of the coast, who are not numerous. But in the 19th century it became a language of caravan trade, and after independence it was made the national language and a required school subject, so the vast majority of Kenyans use it as a second language for communication across ethnic groups.

language.history: Kenya has more than 40 languages, belonging to the Bantu family (Kikuyu, Luhya, Kamba and others), the Nilotic family (Luo, Kalenjin, Maasai and others) and the Cushitic family (Somali and others), reflecting the migrations of different peoples over thousands of years. Swahili is a trade language formed by long contact between the Bantu languages of the East African coast and Arabic, and spread into the interior along caravan routes in the 19th century. During British colonial rule (1895–1963) English became the language of administration and higher education. After independence Swahili was promoted as the national language to unite the peoples, and the 2010 constitution made English and Swahili official languages side by side.

ranking.name: Ugali
ranking.description: A stiff porridge cooked from white maize flour and water, shaped by hand into small balls and dipped into stew or eaten with vegetables. It has a solid texture and mild flavor, and is mainly eaten with stewed meat, vegetables and sauces.
ranking.history: Maize is native to the Americas and was brought to East Africa by the Portuguese after the 16th century, but it became truly widespread in the 20th century under British colonial rule: the colonial government and white-owned farms promoted maize as workers' rations, gradually replacing traditional millet and sorghum. Today ugali is the staple Kenyans eat most, rises and falls in the price of maize are often a political issue, and "a meal without ugali doesn't count" is a common saying.
ranking.imageCredit: Paresh Jai from Nairobi, Kenya・CC BY 2.0・Wikimedia Commons

ranking.name: Nyama choma (grilled meat)
ranking.description: Goat or beef slow-grilled over charcoal and seasoned with salt, often served with a chili-tomato salad (kachumbari) and ugali.
ranking.history: Nyama choma means "grilled meat" in Swahili. Many pastoral peoples of Kenya, such as the Maasai, have counted cattle and sheep as wealth since ancient times, and slaughtering livestock is an important rite. Today grilled meat is at the heart of Kenyan social life: at weekends friends order a kilogram of goat to share at a bar or roadside grill, and holidays such as Independence Day on 12 December (1963) are often celebrated with grilled meat.

ranking.name: Sukuma wiki (sauteed collard greens)
ranking.description: Collard greens are shredded and sauteed or stewed with onion and tomato, a home-style vegetable dish often served with ugali. It tastes light and simple, is cheap, and is a daily side dish for many households.
ranking.history: Sukuma wiki means "push the week" or "stretch the week" in Swahili, reflecting that it is cheap and easy to grow, a vegetable ordinary households rely on to get through until payday. Collard greens were most likely introduced by Europeans in the colonial period and grow easily in the cool climate of Kenya's highlands, and today almost every household garden grows them.
ranking.imageCredit: Paresh Jai from Nairobi, Kenya・CC BY 2.0・Wikimedia Commons

ranking.name: Githeri (maize and bean stew)
ranking.description: Maize kernels and beans are cooked together, sometimes with potatoes, onions and vegetables added, stewed into a single pot. It is plain and nutritionally balanced, and is a home staple in the central region.
ranking.history: Githeri originates among the Kikuyu of the central highlands, traditionally cooked with local beans and maize together, which complement each other nutritionally and keep for a long time. In the colonial and early independence period it was widely used for school lunches and in boarding schools, so many Kenyans have deep childhood memories of it. In the 2017 general election a photo of a man eating githeri while queuing to vote went viral online, and he was dubbed "Githeri Man".

ranking.name: Chapati
ranking.description: A layered flatbread made by kneading flour, oil and water, pan-fried on a griddle until golden, soft and layered. It can be eaten on its own or with stewed beans or stewed meat.
ranking.history: Chapati originates on the Indian subcontinent; when Britain built the Uganda Railway (1896–1901) in the late 19th century it recruited large numbers of laborers from India, and some stayed in Kenya, bringing Indian flatbread culture. Kenyans add more oil and roll it up in layers, making it softer and flakier. Today it is a special food at festivals such as Christmas and at weddings, and is also a common inexpensive street breakfast.
